An acrobatic squirrel in Brooklyn got so spooked when soldiers fired a ceremonial cannon Thursday morning, it hurled itself off a telephone pole — and lived to tell the tale, according to wild footage and officials.

The freaked-out furball threw itself into the air kamikaze-style and plunged dozens of feet after Army members blasted the cannon to welcome a German warship at Fort Hamilton in Brooklyn during America 250 celebrations ahead of the Fourth of July, military officials said.

snippet.title: Pope Leo Receives Liberty Medal and Makes Address for America's 250th Anniversary
snippet.description:
Pope Leo praised the United States' history of welcoming immigrants in his first major address to his home country on Friday (July 3), urging in a video appearance that Americans live up to the ideals put forward in the Declaration of Independence.

The U.S. pope, who has criticised President Donald Trump's hardline anti-immigrant policies as "inhuman", said the word "America" had become a "byword for freedom" across the world because of the way the country welcomed immigrants.

In a speech given live from the Vatican to the National Constitution Center in Philadelphia as he received the Center's Liberty Medal, Leo said he hoped that ideals of "unity, justice and peace" held by the Founding Fathers would guide the U.S. as it celebrated its 250th anniversary.

snippet.title: The Murder in 1790 London: How a Prostitute's Death Changed the Police System
snippet.description:
In the rain-soaked alleys of 1790 Whitechapel, a young woman named Mary Price was found strangled and left for dead. She was a prostitute. She was poor. In the eyes of the city, she was nobody. But her murder would ignite a fire that reshaped the entire British justice system.

This is not just a true crime story. This is the untold origin of modern policing.

When the old parish watchmen failed to catch her killer, and the corrupt reward system proved useless, the London press seized the story. Public outrage erupted. Reformers like Patrick Colquhoun used her case as a weapon in a decades-long battle against a medieval system that protected only the rich. The debates in Parliament pitted liberty against order, tradition against the desperate need for safety. And from that struggle emerged the first professional police force in history, the Metropolitan Police.

Mary Price never knew she would change the world. She was just trying to survive one more night.

In a world full of "goofy ahh," "skibidi," and "Ohio rizz" brainrot, it's only natural to grow tired of TikTok lingo and crave a more refined lexicon to revitalize your silver tongue! With the slang of today leaving much to be desired in the realm of sophistication and potency, one must dive into the history books to study the wonderful words of times past! 

When people today imagine how someone from the 18th century spoke, they tend to imagine a sophisticated and fanciful construction of words, all pieced together masterfully like a work of art. However the reason one would be drawn to this conclusion is actually an example of survivorship bias. Because people today tend to only be familiar with the greatest, most influential, and most classic pieces of literature and writings from the 18th century, we tend to come to the conclusion that everyone around that time must have spoken in a similar way to the writings of the American Declaration of Independence or Gulliver's Travels. But if you were willing to sit down and take the time to study the letters and notes from common folk around this time (or words recorded by observers who are, themselves, literate), you'd find a similar frequency of slang and jargon just like we use today!

 In this video, I explore what the environment of slang, idioms, and jargon looked like in 18th century England, used by the most wretched and cretinous members of society! And maybe, with a bit of societal effort, we can bring some of these phrases back into the spotlight today!

McCarthy, Erin. The Curious Compendium of Wonderful Words. Weldon Owen, 2021.

Richardson, A. E., and Harold Donaldson Eberlein. The English Inn, Past and Present: A Review of Its History and Social Life. B. Blom, 1968.

snippet.title: What life was really like for women in Iran before 1979 | History for sleep
snippet.description:
#history #sleep #historyforsleep

Step into the golden hour of Tehran — sometime in the middle of the twentieth century, when the city smelled of jasmine and saffron, when rooftop radios played slow melodies into the warm evening air, and the women who moved through its wide avenues were living lives far richer and more layered than any single photograph has ever managed to hold.
Tonight, we follow them.

This is a long, slow journey through the quiet textures of women's daily life in Iran before 1979 — told not through headlines or history books, but through the senses. The warmth of a neighbourhood bathhouse at dawn. The amber light of a kitchen where copper pots hold decades of accumulated knowledge. The sound of a record player in a sitting room after dinner, a woman's voice filling the space between walls the way warmth fills a room — gradually, completely, without asking permission.

Along the way, you will sit in a classroom where a first generation of girls copies Hafez into their notebooks. You will move through the cool vaulted lanes of the Grand Bazaar, where women have been conducting quiet commerce for centuries. You will visit a village alleyway where a woman spins wool with hands that carry eight thousand years of practice. You will feel the particular complicated weight of sitting across a kitchen table from a mother who wanted everything for you that she never had for herself.

No drama. No headlines. Just the slow, unhurried texture of ordinary lives, told with care.

This video is designed for listening — in the dark, with your eyes closed, as the day releases its hold and sleep arrives gently at its own pace.

snippet.description:
The 30 Years War fractured Europe and rewrote the rules of power through blood and betrayal. What began as a fierce religious conflict between Catholics and Protestants quickly mutated into a continent-wide struggle for absolute dominance. This historical documentary exposes the hidden realities of the conflict through the eyes of those who lived it.
